terms.gloss: rouse, stir up, call forth (a feeling, laughter, interest)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 3.11.3: quōs ego rīsūs excitāssem!
terms.comment: Its first sense is to wake someone or call him out (ē somnō excitāre); from there, to rouse a person to effort or to call forth a feeling, laughter or a fire (Lewis & Short). Traupman’s word for “excite”.

terms.gloss: stir up, rouse, work up (a crowd, a person, a passion)
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, transitive: the person with ad or in
evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.204 (Lewis & Short): concitārī ad studium cognōscendae percipiendaeque virtūtis
terms.comment: Stronger than excitāre: to set in violent motion, a horse with the spurs, a crowd to arms, a mind to anger or zeal (Lewis & Short). Concitātus is “agitated, worked up”.

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.4: omnēsque incenduntur ad studia glōriā
terms.comment: Literally “set on fire”; of the mind, to fire with zeal, love or anger.
The noun for “excitement”: a stirring of the mind (Lewis & Short, s.v. commōtiō). See also affect, for being moved.

phrases.latin: mihi ille dētur puer, quem laus excitet, quem glōria juvet, quī victus fleat
phrases.english: give me the boy whom praise fires up, who loves glory, who cries when he loses

phrases.latin: honōs alit artēs, omnēsque incenduntur ad studia glōriā
phrases.english: honour feeds the arts, and everyone is fired to effort by glory

phrases.latin: mē miserum, quī nōn adfuerim! quōs ego rīsūs excitāssem!
phrases.english: too bad I wasn’t there! what laughs I’d have raised!
